newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians fall short of fund-raising goal.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians fall short of fund-raising goal.

text.p: Bosnian leaders said on Thursday they still hoped to raise $1.4 billion in post-war aid this year after falling short of their goal at an international donors' conference.

Forty-eight countries and 30 international agencies pledged $1.22 billion in reconstruction aid at a two-day conference which ended in Brussels on Thursday -- less than the $1.4 billion target set by organisers.

"We cannot be dissatisfied with the result of the donors' conference because we are aware that there are many other problems which occupy the world's attention at the moment," said Haris Silajdzic, Moslem co-chairman of the Council of Ministers upon returning to Bosnia.
"If we pay more attention to Bosnian diplomacy there are still chances to reach the promised 1.4 billion dollars by the end of the year," Silajdzic told reporters at Sarajevo airport.
Foreign Trade Minister Hasan Muratovic said he was "surprised" that Islamic countries had not promised more aid to Bosnia, which has enjoyed strong ties with Islamic governments.

Western officials had said before the conference that political paralysis in the country's central government might discourage donors, who committed $1.8 billion last year. Some $1.4 billion of that amount has been delivered.
World Bank officials attending the conference did not say how much aid Bosnia's autonomous Serb entity would receive out of the $1.2 billion.

Some Western officials said the Serb entity would not receive non-humanitarian aid unless authorities handed over former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and other indicted war criminals to a United Nations tribunal.

But international High Representative, Carlos Westerndorp, who oversees the civilian aspects of the peace treaty, has insisted that aid to the Serbs would not be strictly linked to the war criminals issue.

The Serb entity, which covers half the country, has missed out on most of the reconstruction aid flowing to Bosnia so far because nationalist Serb leaders refused to attend last year's conference as part of a joint Bosnian delegation.

Silajdzic said the Moslem-Croat federation and the multi-ethnic central government would receive about 70 percent of the aid and the Serb entity could receive up to 30 percent, pending adherence to the peace agreement.
"However, compliance with the Dayton peace treaty will be the crucial condition for the distribution of funds," he said.
The United States has suggested setting aside funds for the Serb entity until authorities there cooperated with the U.N. war crimes tribunal and allowed non-Serb refugees to return to their homes.
Donors pledged funds for housing projects, restructuring the troubled banking system, social services for returning refugees and repairs to the damaged telephone network.
The World Bank in Sarajevo said foreign firms would soon have the chance to bid on three reconstruction projects requiring management and procurement of equipment and materials.

They said foreign engineering companies would be competing to provide contracting services for a $175 million project to repair roads and bridges, a $65 million aid package for Serb territory and a $29.9 million project for forestry management.
